tasks.task_description: Subproblem 1 (spread prediction). Determine whether and how precisely the geographic spread of Vespa mandarinia over time can be predicted from the sighting data. Scope: use the confirmed (lab-verified) positive detections to characterize the spatial and temporal footprint of the invasion in Washington State, and to state the range of distances and rates the pest has actually moved.
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions: (a) 'Positive ID' reports are the only reliable ground truth for true spread, because Negative/Unverified/Unprocessed reports are dominated by mistaken identification of other hornets; (b) the first Washington confirmed detection (2019-09-30, Skagit County, lat 48.994 lon -122.702) is the local origin of the Washington cluster (the 2019-09-19 positive at 49.149,-123.943 is the original Vancouver Island colony, across the border, and is treated as the seed event, not part of the in-state spread); (c) spread is driven by queens establishing new nests within their flight range, so the spread is a bounded radial process rather than a random walk. Method: I characterize the confirmed footprint rather than fitting a stochastic diffusion, because with only 13 in-state positives a parametric spread model (e.g. a 2D diffusion constant) would be severely under-identified; descriptive statistics with interval estimates are the statistically sound level of inference here. I compute the pairwise distances among confirmed positives, the radius of the cluster, and the detection timeline, and compare the observed footprint to the biologically reported 30 km queen range.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Let P = {p_i} be the 13 Washington confirmed positives with coordinates (lat_i, lon_i) and dates d_i. Use the haversine distance d(a,b) = 2R arcsin( sqrt( sin^2((lat_a-lat_b)/2) + cos(lat_a)cos(lat_b) sin^2((lon_a-lon_b)/2) ) ), R = 6371 km. Define the cluster centroid c = (mean lat, mean lon) and the cluster radius r = max_i d(p_i, c). Define the spread diameter D = max_{i,j} d(p_i, p_j). Timeline: first detection d_min, last d_max, span T = (d_max - d_min). Parameter table (empirical inputs): queen_nest_range = 30 km, interval [25, 35], source: problem statement (Penn State Extension background) with supporting refs DOI 10.3389/finsc.2023.1145158 (invasion potential of Vespa spp.) and DOI 10.1002/ece3.4182 (worker action/foraging range). All distances below are computed from the dataset.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: The 13 in-state confirmed positives span 2019-09-30 to 2020-10-01 (T = 12.1 months). The cluster centroid is (48.970, -122.635) with max radius r = 26.6 km and spread diameter D = 39.8 km. This footprint is fully consistent with a single establishment (Vancouver Island seed) plus a chain of new nests each within the ~30 km queen range: every new positive lies within ~27 km of the cluster core, and the total 40 km diameter is a handful of sequential 30 km hops over 12 months, not a continuous expansion. Precision: the observed spread is predictable only to within the queen-range unit (~30 km) per generation/season; the data do not support a sub-10 km localization of where the next nest will form, because positives are sparse (13) and clustered. What IS predictable: (1) new confirmed detections are overwhelmingly likely to fall within ~30-40 km of the existing cluster (all 13 do); (2) detections are strongly seasonal, concentrated in the active fall window; (3) the geographic 'front' expands on the order of one queen-range per active season. Limitation/bias: 13 points is too few to estimate a diffusion constant or a direction of spread with confidence; the Washington positives are concentrated in Skagit County, so the model under-covers the rest of the state, and the single Vancouver Island seed is an outlier that inflates the all-positive diameter to 118.7 km if included.

tasks.task_description: Subproblem 2 (misan-classification model). Build, analyze, and discuss a model that predicts the likelihood that a public report is a mistaken identification (i.e., NOT Vespa mandarinia), using only the provided dataset and image files. Scope: a supervised model trained on the 2048 lab-confirmed reports (14 Positive ID = true hornet, 2034 Negative ID = mistaken) that outputs P(report is true Vespa) for any report.
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions: (a) the lab labels Positive ID and Negative ID are the ground truth (Unverified/Unprocessed are excluded from training but scored at inference); (b) the target is binary: y=1 true Vespa, y=0 mistaken ID of another insect; (c) a report's likelihood of being true is driven by (i) proximity to already-confirmed hornets (spatial clustering of a real invasion), (ii) time-of-year (hornets are active/detectable in the fall season, and the invasion was detected in fall), (iii) whether a specimen or clear image was submitted (the diagnostic feature is the specimen's head morphology — a massive orange-yellow head — which a size-only report does not carry; this was confirmed by domain expertise that size alone misleads), (iv) note length (dramatic long reports skew toward mistaken IDs). Method: logistic regression with standardized features and a balanced class weight (the 14:2034 imbalance would otherwise collapse the model to 'all negative'). I chose logistic regression over a tree/NN because with 14 positives a high-capacity model would overfit the positives; a linear model with few features is the most defensible, interpretable, and out-of-sample-robust choice. Validation: leave-one-out on all 14 positives, plus repeated stratified 5-fold (50 splits), plus a time-series split and a spatial split.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Logistic model: logit[P(y=1|x)] = w0 + sum_k w_k * z_k(x), where z_k are standardized features (z = (x - mean)/sd, standardized on the training set). Features and fitted coefficients (C = 1.0, class_weight balanced, intercept w0 = -17.91): z(dist_to_nearest_confirmed) coefficient -4.54 (dominant; log1p-transformed); z(dist_to_origin) -0.23; z(days_since_origin) -0.45; z(season_fall) +0.50; z(note_len) -0.68; z(has_specimen) +0.41; z(mentions_bee_harm) -0.56; z(n_images) -1.08; z(max_image_dim) +0.17; z(max_file_size) -0.22. Distance features are log1p-transformed before standardization. dist_to_nearest_confirmed and dist_to_origin use haversine with R=6371 km; the origin is the first Washington positive (2019-09-30). has_specimen = 1 if the notes mention a specimen/'sent to lab'. Goodness of fit: repeated 5-fold AUC = 1.000 (sd 0.000), AP = 1.000; leave-one-out: all 14 positives scored P >= 0.848 (median 0.995), all 200 sampled negatives scored P <= 0.212 (mean 0.0019) — no overlap, so the model separates confirmed classes out-of-sample. In-sample confusion at threshold 0.5: TP=14, FN=0, FP=4, TN=2030 (precision 0.778, recall 1.000).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: The model shows that a report's probability of being a true Vespa is governed almost entirely by spatial context: the single strongest signal (coefficient -4.54) is closeness to an already-confirmed hornet. A report within ~1-2 km of a known cluster in the fall season with a specimen gets P near 1.0; the same description 150+ km away gets P near 0. The overall base rate is very low: among all confirmed reports, P(true Vespa) = 14/2048 = 0.0068, Wilson 95% CI [0.0041, 0.0114], so the misclassification rate is 0.9932, CI [0.9886, 0.9959] — about 99% of confirmed reports are mistaken IDs, which is exactly the problem's premise. Seasonal breakdown: the fall positive rate is 0.020 (CI [0.011, 0.038]) vs 0.003 outside fall, so a fall report is ~7x more likely to be true. Limitations and biases: (1) n_pos = 14 is tiny, so individual coefficient magnitudes are uncertain even though the ordering and the perfect separation are stable under LOO; (2) the spatial features create a circularity — the model is best where hornets have already been confirmed, so it is a prioritization/incremental tool, not a way to find the very first hornet in a virgin area; (3) the image features (n_images, max_dim) add little because most reports have one phone photo and the true diagnostic (head morphology) is not captured by file size or pixel dimensions; (4) the model inherits the lab's label bias — it learns 'what the lab confirmed', not the true prevalence, and it cannot see reports the public never submitted.

tasks.task_description: Subproblem 3 (prioritization). Use the classification model to produce a strategy for prioritizing public reports for follow-up investigation, given the limited resources of the state agencies. Scope: a concrete, actionable ordering of the unverified reports and a decision rule for dispatching field resources.
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions: (a) the state can only act on a handful of reports concurrently — roughly 1 to 2 dispatchable inspectors at any moment, a small dedicated unit rather than a fleet (domain expertise; see field_crew_capacity in the parameter table) — so the deliverable must be a total priority ordering, not a fixed-size batch; (b) a report is only confirmable if a specimen or clear image is available, because the lab confirmation rests on the head morphology of a specimen — so a report that is geographically promising but has no specimen is a lower-priority 're-contact the reporter' action than one with a specimen; (c) follow-up should be concentrated in the active season. Method: score every Unverified report with the fitted logistic model (transformed by the training-time mean/sd), rank in descending order of P(true Vespa), and dispatch the top of the queue to the available crews. Because the capacity is ~2 concurrent, the output is a ranked queue plus a score distribution over the top K to show how quickly the signal decays.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: For each unverified report r, compute s(r) = P(y=1 | x_r) from the fitted model (same feature construction, standardized by the training mean/sd). Sort unverified reports by s descending: r_(1) >= r_(2) >= ... >= r_(2208). The dispatch rule is: assign the single next-highest unprocessed report to a free crew, and re-rank after each lab result (see subproblem 4). A 'confirmable' report (has specimen or clear image) outranks a same-region report that is size-only, all else equal. I report the score profile of the ranked queue: top-10 scores [0.951, 0.999] (median 0.975), top-25 [0.784, 0.999] (median 0.944), top-50 [0.367, 0.999] (median 0.773), top-100 [0.076, 0.999] (median 0.362). The top of the queue is dominated by reports within ~1-10 km of confirmed clusters in the fall season.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: The strategy concentrates the agency's scarce field time where confirmation is both likely and possible. The top-ranked unverified reports are, e.g., a 2020-10-03 report 9.2 km from the origin (score 0.999), a 2019-10-15 report 0.9 km from origin that mentions bee harm (0.999), and a cluster of 2020-09 reports 5-32 km out (0.97-0.99). Because the realistic concurrency is only ~1-2 crews, the agency should not 'work down a list of 100'; it should always know the single next report and re-rank after each result, which also naturally front-loads the fall season (the top-100 contains 27 fall reports, and the fall rate is ~7x the off-season rate). Practical guidance: (1) dispatch the top 1-2 reports immediately; (2) for a high-score report lacking a specimen, the fastest action is to re-contact the reporter to secure a specimen or a clearer photo rather than drive out; (3) deprioritize size-only reports far from clusters even if dramatic, because the misclassification base rate there is ~99%. Limitation: the ranking is only as good as the model's spatial prior — it will under-rank the first true hornet in a genuinely new area (no nearby confirmed positive), which is precisely the report the state most wants. This is the inherent tension of a data-driven prioritization rule and is mitigated by keeping a small random/stratified sample of far reports for surveillance.

tasks.task_description: Subproblems 4 and 5 (model updating and eradication evidence). (4) How the model should be updated as new reports arrive over time, and how often. (5) Using the model, what would constitute evidence that the pest has been eradicated in Washington State.
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions: (a) new lab results (reports that move from Unverified to Positive/Negative) are the only new supervision, and they arrive on the lab's processing schedule; (b) the model's spatial prior must grow as new confirmed positives are added, because the 'distance to nearest confirmed' feature is defined relative to the confirmed set; (c) eradication is a statistical claim about the absence of a persistent population, and it requires both passive-reporting evidence and active-surveillance evidence, with continued reporting as a precondition so that silence means absence rather than lost surveillance. Method: a retraining rule keyed to the arrival of new confirmed labels and to seasonal boundaries; and an eradication rule combining a no-positive window with maintained reporting volume and targeted-surveillance zeros.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Update rule: (i) Add each new Positive ID to the confirmed set P so that dist_to_nearest_confirmed and dist_to_origin are recomputed for all unscored reports (this is a data update, O(n) per new positive). (ii) Refit the logistic coefficients when the number of new confirmed positives since the last fit reaches a threshold, or at each season boundary (spring emergence and fall active window), whichever comes first; with ~14 positives the coefficient set is sensitive, so refit after every batch of >=3-5 new confirmed positives, and always refit across the winter->spring transition when the colony cycle restarts. (iii) Keep the scaler (mean/sd) and features fixed unless the feature set changes, to keep scores comparable over time. Lab turnaround from the data: for reports where submission date exceeds detection date, the median lag is 3 days (p90 242 days, mean 104 days); 64% are same-day (state employees), so a weekly re-score of the unverified queue is the natural cadence, with a full refit at least seasonally. Eradication rule (joint): declare eradication only if ALL hold: (A) zero confirmed (lab- or genetic-) positives for 2-3 consecutive full seasons, each including a spring emergence and a fall reproductive cycle; (B) public reporting volume stays at a normal baseline throughout (surveillance still live) — the reporting stream continuing is what makes the silence meaningful; (C) targeted surveillance (traps, checks of known/suspected sites) returns zero workers and zero nests; any new confirmed worker or nest voids the count and starts the 2-3 season window again. Quantitative backing: with the measured fall positive rate p = 0.020 (upper 95% bound 0.038), the probability of 0 confirmed positives in n confirmed reports is (1-p)^n = 0.144 at n=100 and 4.3e-4 at n=200 for p=0.038; so requiring a full fall season of active confirmed testing with zero positives, repeated for 2-3 seasons, makes the false-'eradicat-ed' probability negligible. Parameter table (empirical inputs): fall_positive_rate = 0.020, interval [0.011, 0.038], source: computed from the dataset (9 fall positives / 450 fall confirmed reports, Wilson CI); queen_nest_range = 30 km, interval [25,35], source: problem statement with DOI 10.3389/finsc.2023.1145158 and DOI 10.1002/ece3.4182; field_crew_capacity = 2, interval [1,2], source: expert exchange 2 (agency practice); eradication_window_seasons = 3, interval [2,3], source: expert exchange 3 (agency practice), calibrated to the fall positive-rate CI above.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: The update schedule is driven by two clocks: the lab's result feed (re-score the queue weekly; add new positives to the confirmed set immediately so the spatial prior stays current) and the biology's seasons (refit at the spring/fall boundaries and after >=3-5 new confirmed positives). This is robust to the lab's uneven turnaround (median 3 days but p90 242 days) because the re-score is cheap and the refit is infrequent. For eradication, the decision is deliberately conservative: a single quiet year is NOT evidence (the pest is seasonal and can overwinter in the soil), and passive-report silence alone is NOT evidence (it could be lost surveillance). The joint rule — 2-3 full seasons of zero confirmed positives with reporting at a normal baseline and zero workers/nests from targeted traps — is the level of negative evidence that, at the measured fall detection rate, reduces the false-negative probability below 10^-3. Limitation: the eradication criterion assumes the state maintains the same reporting channels and surveillance effort; if the public stops reporting (channel fatigue), the rule's precondition (B) fails and the claim cannot be made, which is the correct behavior but means eradication can never be declared faster than the slowest of (surveillance, public trust, seasons). The model's spatial prior also means that after eradication, a single new report in a previously virgin area would be under-scored by the old confirmed-set, so the surveillance traps (not the model) are the backstop that catches re-establishment.
